Aseptic loosening–associated pain and osteolysis is the primary reason for midterm and long-
term revision total joint replacement and is responsible for more than 70% of total hip
arthroplasty revision procedures and more than 44% of total knee arthroplasty revision
procedures.1,2
Implant debris–induced biologic inflammatory reactions (mediated by cytokines) have been
well established as the central cause of long-term implant failure.2,3
Local bone loss (or peri-implant osteolysis) is initiated via aseptic inflammatory responses to
implant debris, primarily mediated by phagocytosis of small implant wear particles (generally
<1 to 5 μm in diameter), resulting in the release of inflammatory and osteolytic cytokines that
increase bone loss and loss of implant-tissue integrity.4-6
Inflammatory cytokines are produced by innate and adaptive immune cells and all peri-
implant tissue cells (eg, fibroblasts, osteoblasts).
Not all cytokines are created equally. Some are far more potent than others (eg, interleukin
[IL]-1ß and tumor necrosis factor [TNF]-α) and are tightly regulated by secretion/production
inhibition, auto-degradation mechanisms, and anti-inflammatory cytokines (eg, IL-4, IL-10, IL-1
receptor antagonist).
Overview
Cytokines are small proteins (approximately 5 to 25 kDa) that are generated by various cells in
the body, typically in response to an activating stimulus, and they elicit biologic responses by
binding to specific receptors.
Cytokines can act in an autocrine, paracrine, and endocrine manner.
Cytokines include chemokines but not hormones or growth factors.
Cytokines are produced by bone, tissue, and immune cells, all of which are central to
orthopaedics (ie, peri-implant), particularly host immune responses to infection, inflammation,
trauma, infection, cancer, and reactivity to implants and implant debris.
Cytokine release is stimulus dependent (eg, bacteria versus implant debris) and coordinates
the host immune defense (ie, the released cytokines can recruit and activate different types of
effector cells).
Central cytokines are involved in innate and adaptive inflammatory reactions to bone/tissue
damage, healing, and implant (debris) reactivity.

Overview
Cytokines are a loosely defined category of small proteins (approximately 5 to 25 kDa)
central to cell signaling by binding to specific cell surface receptors. Some cytokines are
membrane-bound and/or transported and produced by secreted extracellular vesicles,
complicating the differentiation between cytokine and receptor roles. Essentially,
cytokines cannot passively penetrate cell membranes and do not act on cells without
specific receptors for that cytokine. Cytokines can act in an autocrine, paracrine, and
endocrine manner, primarily as immunomodulating agents controlling central functions,
such as cell activation, metabolism, proliferation, apoptosis, pyroptosis, movement, etc.;
however, in orthopaedics, their mechanism of action and influence are primarily local
(autocrine and paracrine) rather than systemic (endocrine).
Cytokines include chemokines, interferons (IFNs), ILs, lymphokines, and TNFs. Cytokines
can be classified into broad families that share activation mechanisms and protein
structural features, but they can have remarkably diverse functions (eg, the TNF/TNF
receptor superfamily, IL-1 superfamily, and IL-6 superfamily).
Cytokine effectiveness depends on cytokine receptors and how these receptors
transduce cytokine binding intracellularly. Cytokine receptors are cell-surface
glycoproteins that bind to specific cytokines, even at exceptionally low cytokine
concentrations; these processes are not reversible. Classification schemes for these
receptors are cumbersome and generally based on the three-dimensional structure in
which most inflammatory cytokines bind to type I or type II cytokine receptors or TNF-
type receptors. Cytokine transduction commonly occurs via an intracellular signaling
pathway known as Janus kinase (JAK)-signal transducer and activator of transcription
proteins (STAT) pathway. The binding of cytokines, such as IFNs and ILs to cell surface
receptors leads to dimerization of receptors and the direct binding of receptor-
associated JAK intracellular domains. The JAK-STAT pathway is central in relaying signals
from the cell-membrane receptors to the nucleus. The JAK-STAT pathway is central for
many cytokines, IFNs, and growth factors, resulting in critical cellular events, such as
immune system development and hematopoiesis. All four JAK pathway subtypes have
overlapping receptor responsibilities. This is important in orthopaedics because drugs

that inhibit an enzyme family (also known as jakinibs) currently are used to manage
inflammatory/autoimmune diseases, such as rheumatoid arthritis. Therefore, targeting
The JAK-STAT pathway as a therapeutic strategy to block proinflammatory cytokines,
such as IL-6, which is commonly overexpressed in numerous immune-mediated and
inflammatory diseases, is gaining popularity and indications for use.7
Cytokines do not include hormones or growth factors despite some similar effects and
mechanisms of action. The clear lack of endocrine action associated with orthopaedic
cytokines makes this distinction clear. Cytokines are effectively produced by all cells in
the peri-implant space, including all local immune cells (eg, macrophages, B
lymphocytes, T lymphocytes, mast cells), tissue cells (eg, fibroblasts, various stromal
cells), and bone/cartilage cells (eg, osteoblasts, osteoclasts, and osteocytes). Each cell
type can only produce certain cytokines. Some cytokines are produced by only one type
of cell, and these generally are regarded as signature cytokines for that cell type.
Cytokines act via cell surface receptors and are a cornerstone of immune reactivity.
Cytokines are essential components in health and fighting disease, particularly host
immune responses to infection, inflammation, trauma, cancer, and reactivity to
orthopaedic implant debris. Central cytokines are involved in innate and adaptive
inflammatory reactions to tissue healing and orthopaedic implant–induced reactivity (ie,
implant debris).
Normal Cytokine Response in Wound/Fracture Healing
Immediate proinflammatory response: The primary cytokines that immediately act in response
to bone fracture or orthopaedic implant placement are IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, chemokine (C-C motif)
ligand (CCL) 2, and others.
After acute inflammation, a shift to less inflammation is mediated by a shift to anti-
inflammatory cytokine production (eg, IL-4, IL-10, IL-1 receptor antagonist, and IL-13) to control
or prevent chronic inflammation and local and systemic tissue damage.
Repair response: A balance between osteoblastic and osteoclastic activity is controlled by
cytokines, such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, which control long-term bone homeostasis and, in
general, the performance of orthopaedic implants.

Acute-Phase Cytokines

Acute-Phase Cytokines
The inflammatory response that immediately follows bone fracture or orthopaedic
implant placement and any associated hematomas/blood clotting scaffolds leads to
various recruited inflammatory cells and release of associated cytokines, such as IL-1, IL-
6, TNF-α, CCL2, and others, which form the basis of an acute inflammatory response8
(Figure 1). Innate immune cells, such as polymorphonuclear leukocytes and monocytes,
extravasate from local blood vessels and infiltrate the areas where tissue damage has
occurred (ie, fracture or implant site).9,10 Macrophages are activated to a more
proinflammatory phenotype (polarized to M1 macrophages) and release a cascade of
cytokines and induce production of several proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1ß, IL-
6, TNF-α, and IFN-γ. After infiltration of monocytes/macrophages, the innate immune
system recruits cells from the adaptive immune system (lymphocytes) to the site of
damage for immunosurveillance of specific pathogens that may be responsible. This
process initially is the result of the activation of resident macrophages, resulting in tissue
inflammation and cell recruitment because of the extravasation of innate immune cells,
such as neutrophils and monocytes, to the site of inflammation and tissue damage. This
then forms an inflammatory attractor as monocytes mature into tissue macrophages
and become activated. The result is the recruitment of additional inflammatory cells to
the tissue, and the initial inflammatory response is maintained and reinforced8 (Figure
1).

Figure 1 Schematic of bone/tissue healing for fractures and implant placement shows
the dominant cytokines expressed during three basic stages. Cytokines are primarily
produced by immune cells. Early pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interleukin (IL)-1,
IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α, are necessary for bone fracture healing in the
early and repair/remodeling phases; however, the same cytokines that typically are
expressed in the latter stages of repair and maintenance may be overexpressed, leading
to unwanted inflammation that compromises biologic implant performance. The ability
to shift or shut down these proinflammatory actions by anti-inflammatory cytokines also
is central to bone fracture repair, implant integration, and longer term implant fixation.

Repair-Phase Cytokines

Repair-Phase Cytokines
After acute local tissue inflammation, a transition to less inflammation is mediated by a
shift to anti-inflammatory cytokine production (eg, IL-4, IL-10, and IL-13) by cells such as
SEND FEEDBACK

anti-inflammatory macrophages, also termed M2 macrophages. The degree to which
these cells can be transformed from an inflammatory M1 macrophage to an anti-
inflammatory M2 macrophage phenotype is mediated by cytokines, such as IL-4 and IL-
13. Bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells are chemotactically drawn by cytokines, such
as TNF-α and chemokine (C-X-C motif) ligand 12, to the site of tissue inflammation.8
These stem cells and inflammatory cells use complex cytokine communication to induce
the production of growth factors (transforming growth factor [TGF]-ß, bone
morphogenetic proteins, vascular endothelial growth factor [VEGF], platelet-derived
growth factor, and fibroblast growth factor-2) to facilitate fibrogenesis, osteogenesis, and
angiogenesis of new blood vessels.11
Healing and Bone Maintenance Cytokines or Chronic Inflammation

Healing and Bone Maintenance Cytokines or Chronic Inflammation
During the latter stages of implant-bone integration or general bone healing, a balance
between osteoblastic and osteoclastic activity is regained and controlled largely by
mitigating cytokines, such as IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-α, which can be expressed in the peri-
implant/bone milieu.9,12-14 The degree to which these cytokines revert to a higher or
lower inflammatory state depends on the interaction of an individual’s immune system
with resultant implant debris or other stimuli. If not appropriately mitigated or if
continually provoked, higher levels of cytokines, such as IL-1 and TNF-α, can induce a
state of chronic inflammation. Therefore, long-term remodeling-phase cytokines can
largely mediate the long-term performance and success of orthopaedic implants.
Innate Immune Cytokine Response in Orthopaedics
Initial Mechanisms for Wear Particle–Related Activation of the Innate
Immune System

Innate immune response to implant debris primarily mediates inflammatory cytokine
production to the site of total joint arthroplasty and is responsible for associated osteolysis
and implant loosening.
M1 macrophages tend to dominate the response to an implant debris challenge.
M1 cytokines include IL-1α, IL-1ß, IL-6, IL-10, IL-11, IL-15, TNF-α, TGF-α, granulocyte-
macrophage colony stimulating factor, macrophage colony stimulating factor (M-CSF), platelet-
derived growth factor, and epidermal growth factor.15
Chemokines, such as IL-8, monocyte chemoattractant protein (MCP)-1, macrophage
inflammatory protein (MIP)-1a, CCL17/thymus and activation-related chemokine (TARC), and
CCL22/macrophage-derived chemokine (MDC),16 are produced by immune cells (eg,
macrophages) and tissue cells (eg, fibroblasts and osteoblasts).17-21
Effective immune system activation and cytokine response require specific pattern recognition
receptors that recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and DAMPs.
Nuclear factor kappa beta (NF-κß) is a central transcription factor that is a critical mediator of
inflammatory responses by inducing the expression of proinflammatory cytokines and
chemokines.22,23
The signaling pathways activated by the interaction of PAMPs and DAMPs with cognate pattern
recognition receptors lead to NF-κß activation in the nucleus and the upregulation of
transcription factors of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines.22,23
PAMP recognition is associated with cytokines, such as TNF-α, IL-1ß, and IL-12.22
DAMPs activate inflammasome danger signaling nod-like intracellular receptors (NLR family)
and NF-κß, resulting in release of potent inflammatory cytokines IL-1ß, IL-18, and IL-33.24

Initial Mechanisms for Wear Particle–Related Activation of the
Innate Immune System
The central immune response (and general biologic response) to implant debris limiting
the long-term performance of orthopaedic implants is to the result of innate immune
reactivity that is primarily driven by macrophage reactivity to damage-associated
molecular patterns (DAMPs); this then elicits cytokine-based inflammatory macrophage
immune responses.

Macrophages

Macrophages
Innate immune inflammatory responses to implant debris are mainly attributed to
macrophage reactivity and have been the primary focus of investigation over the past 40
years. M1 macrophages tend to dominate the response to an implant debris challenge
(released metal ions and particles) by producing proinflammatory cytokines that act in
an autocrine and paracrine fashion about implants8,25 (Figure 1). After contact with
orthopaedic implant debris, macrophages generally polarize to an M1 phenotype and
can release many M1-associated cytokines. M1 cytokines include IL-1α, IL-1ß, IL-6, IL-10,
IL-11, IL-15, TNF-α, TGF-α, granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor, M-CSF,
platelet-derived growth factor, and epidermal growth factor8,9,15 (Figure 1). More subtle
macrophage (M1) cytokines and tissue responses likely are involved in this reactivity as
well but remain unknown. The actions of these cytokines are multifunctional, complex,
and not fully understood. They can act directly on bone, affecting remodeling via the
induction of M-CSF and other stimulating factors that activate the formation of
osteoclasts. Proinflammatory M1 cytokines, such as IL-1, TNF-α, and IL-6, can affect
osteoblasts and other cells that that activate osteoclasts and act indirectly in a positive
feedback manner to increase cytokine release by macrophages.15 Other cytokines can
act indirectly on bone (eg, granulocyte-macrophage colony stimulating factor is
responsible for formation of multinucleated giant cells, which act similar to osteoclasts).
Chemokine expression resulting from implant debris is not limited to immune cells (eg,
macrophages); fibroblasts and osteoblasts exposed to implant debris also are central
mediators of biologic responses to implant debris.17-21 Potent chemokines, activated by
implant debris and implicated in aseptic loosening pathology, include IL-8, MCP-1 MIP-
1α, CCL17/TARC, and CCL22/MDC16 and are released by macrophages and mesenchymal
stem cells in periprosthetic tissues in response to different types of implant debris,
including titanium, cobalt-chromium-molybdenum alloy, ultra-high–molecular-weight
polyethylene, and others.25,26 These chemokines lead to the migration of macrophages
and osteoclasts to the bone-implant region and may potentiate aseptic inflammatory
induced osteolysis.16,18 Although MIP-1α is more macrophage specific, MCP-1 also is

respectively, has been shown to stop the migration of mesenchymal stem cells in vitro
and decrease recruitment of osteoclast precursors to the bone-implant interface;27 this

PAMP recognition is associated with specific pattern recognition receptors (ie, toll-like
receptors), which are necessary for infection-fighting cytokine release profiles. These
same responses also may be responsible for excessive debris-induced aseptic
loosening.30-32 This has been determined using toll-like receptor and IL-1 receptor
knockout mouse models (MyD88 knockout-mice), in which lower numbers of cytokines
are produced and polymethyl methacrylate implant debris particle–induced osteolysis is
mitigated.16,33 Toll-like receptor and IL-1 receptor signaling results in MyD88-dependent
pathway activation of central transcription factor NF-κß , which plays a central role in
particle-induced osteolysis via direct and indirect production of proinflammatory
cytokines, such as TNF-α, IL-1ß, and IL-1222 (Figure 2). In addition, DAMPs and cytokines
that are released as a result of cell stress, damage, inflammation, and cell death may
elicit a positive feedback immune response by activating NF-κß. Therefore, in the context
of implant debris (particles and ions), NF-κß and NLRP3 inflammasome can be directly
and indirectly activated via mechanisms such as lysosomal rupture and release of
reactive oxygen species22,23 (Figure 2). In addition, the activation of NF-κß in the nucleus
leads to more transcription of inactive pro forms of cytokines, such as IL-1ß and IL-18 (ie,
pro-IL-1ß and pro-IL-18), which will remain nondegraded in the cytoplasm in their
inactive forms until activated22,23,34 (Figure 2).

Inflammasome Danger Signaling Cytokines

Inflammasome Danger Signaling Cytokines
Cell or tissue damage results in danger signaling (ie, inflammasome activation), in which
nonpathogen-derived (ie, sterile) stimuli activate immune cells via central components

termed the inflammasome.35
After implant debris activates the inflammasome pathway (via macrophage phagocytosis
of wear debris), cells release mature IL-1ß, IL-18, IL-33, and other cytokines and
chemokines as follows:
Implant debris (ions and particulate) → phagocytosis → lysosome damage → reactive
oxygen species production → inflammasome activation (NACHT-, LRR-, and pyrin
domain–containing protein [NALP] 3/apoptosis-associated speck-like protein containing
a C-terminal caspase recruitment domain [ASC]) → caspase 1 → mature IL-1ß secretion
and secretion of other IL-1-family cytokines and chemokines (eg, MCP-1)
Effective immune system activation and cytokine response require specific receptors
that recognize PAMPs and DAMPs8,9,34,36 (Figures 1 and 2). Examples of nonpathogen-
derived danger signals are ultraviolet light, gout crystals, particulate adjuvants present in
vaccines,37,38 and implant debris.39 Orthopaedic implant debris largely triggers
inflammasome activation via lysosomal destabilization after phagocytosis by cells such
as macrophages and fibroblasts, which causes an increase in intracellular nicotinamide
adenine dinucleotide phosphate-oxidase and an increase in intracellular reactive oxygen
species.38,40,41 The release of these intracellular contents is sensed by a specific NLR
family, which normally is inhibited but becomes activated under stress, danger, or
damage conditions and oligomerizes to form the inflammasome complex, such as
NALP3.42,43 Activation of the inflammasome complex (NALP-ASC complex) leads to the
cleavage of inactive pro-caspase-1 into active caspase-1. This active caspase is required
for the conversion of inactive to active proinflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1ß and IL-
18, via cleaving intracellular pro-IL-1ß, pro-IL-18, and others into their active mature
forms. IL-1ß likely is the main cytokine responsible for mediating inflammatory aseptic
osteolysis44 because macrophage release of IL-1ß has potent consequences, such as
receptor activator of NF-κß (RANK) ligand induction that hampers bone remodeling.
Toxicity responses to implant debris are another facet of innate immune activation, in
which apoptosis-associated cytokines and hypoxia responses have been found.45-47
Soluble and particulate metal debris can induce hypoxia-like pathology, as measured by

identify the manner in which (via noncarcinogenic means) local soft tissue growths (fibro-

ceramic and polyethylene implant debris particles have been shown to induce some

fibroblast-mediated growths in vivo (ie, pseudotumors).45,46 These hypoxia and
apoptosis responses are associated with cytokines such as IL-1α, TNF-α, IL-8, MCP-1),
intercellular adhesion molecule-1, and IFN-1.48,49
Adaptive Immune Cytokine Response in Orthopaedics
Adaptive immune responses to implant debris, although far less prevalent than innate
immune responses, may occur and become clinically relevant in some orthopaedic patients.
In general, adaptive immune responses to implant debris are mediated by T and B
lymphocytes and their cytokines.50,53
More specifically, implant debris–associated adaptive immune responses involve the effector
subsets of T helper (Th) cells, including Th1 (IFN-γ and IL-2) and Th17 cells (IL-17).54,55
Th1 or Th17 cells also can recruit and continue to activate macrophages, with relatively few
participating T cells required.
Th (Th1 and Th17) immune responses are classified as type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity
(DTH) responses.
Peripheral blood can be used to test the adaptive immune response to implant debris,
including cytokine production.
These excessive/unwanted adaptive immune cytokine responses may lead to premature
implant failure.
Soluble and particulate metal debris may induce hypoxia-like pathologic changes as measured
by HIF-1a and VEGF.47

Adaptive Immune Cytokine Response in Orthopaedics
Adaptive immune responses to implant debris are mediated by lymphocytes, and T and
B lymphocytes and their associated cytokines occasionally are present in peri-implant
tissues.50,53 Implant debris–induced adaptive immune responses mainly involve Th cells
(not T cytotoxic/suppressor).61 The Th subset, Th1 cells, have been identified by their
signature cytokine production of IFN-γ and IL-2, and to a lesser degree IL-17, fractalkine,
and cluster of differentiation (CD) 40, which indicate Th17 activity (versus non-observed
Th2 cell–mediated IL-10 responses).54,55 Specific cytokine responses of Th1 or Th17 cells
also can recruit and activate macrophages with relatively few participating T cells,
suggesting that the adaptive immune response has a substantial role that may be easily
overlooked. This underscores the likelihood of adaptive immune response participation
in peri-implant pathologic inflammation if lymphocyte aggregates are identified locally,
particularly of identified histologically in an activated state by cytokines or surface
markers59,60 (Figure 3); however, this may be underreported because it is not
considered standard of care to evaluate for or identify these responses in peri-implant
tissues via signature cytokines and receptors, such as IL-2, IL-17, IFN-γ, and TNF-α.62-64
Innate and adaptive immune feedback and crosstalk (eg, macrophages and lymphocytes)
also interact via co-receptors and cytokines that are reported less often, such as IL-15
and its related IL-15 receptor (IL-15 receptor alpha) on macrophages and IL-2 receptor
(IL-2 receptor ß) on lymphocytes,65 and costimulatory molecules (CD80, CD86,
intracellular adhesion molecule-1) that are crucial for adaptive lymphocyte responses.66

Although little objection exists to acknowledging adaptive immune response
participation in implant debris reactivity, a reluctance exists to acknowledge that these
Th responses are, by definition, a type IV DTH response. This may be rooted in
uncertainty with regard to which clonally specific metal-antigen sensitized and activated
DTH T cells exist; however, regardless of specificity, the result is the same and is
characteristic of a DTH response in which lymphocytes release various cytokines that
further recruit and activate macrophages56,60 (Figure 3). These include the following
potent cytokines: monocyte chemotactic activating factor (induces chemotaxis of
monocytes to areas of DTH activation), IFN-γ and TNF-ß (affects facilitation of infiltration
by local endothelial cells), and migration inhibitory factor (inhibits migration of
macrophages and encourages them to stay in the local area of the DTH reaction). After
activation, macrophages have an increased ability to present major histocompatibility
complex class II and release IL-2, which may trigger the activation of more T-DTH cells;
these then act in a positive feedback cycle to recruit and activate more macrophages,
which recruit and activate more T-DTH cells and so on. Therefore, without T-regulatory
cells and their associated cytokines to control and end this cycle, even a subtle adaptive
immune response has the potential to become extreme, and DTH self-perpetuating
responses may induce extensive tissue damage. Although isolation of lymphocytes from
the peri-implant space (eg, biopsy) is not practically possible, peripheral blood can be
used to test the adaptive immune response to implant debris, including cytokine
production. Cytokine testing and metal DTH testing via the lymphocyte transformation
test require isolating peripheral blood mononuclear cells from a normal blood draw and
exposing the isolated cells to specific suspect challenge agents (such as cobalt or nickel)
over a minimum of 4 to 7 days; this allows for a delayed-type reactivity to occur that
enables diagnosis of individuals who may have a predisposition or an active adaptive
immune response to implant metals, bone cement monomer, etc. These excessive
and/or unwanted adaptive immune cytokine responses may lead to premature implant
failure (approximately >1% to 2% of total joint arthroplasty recipients per 3 to 5 years at
<5 years postoperatively) but are vital to protect against peri-implant infection.38


Osteoclasts
Osteoclasts are central to cytokine-induced osteolysis given that they are the primary
bone resorbing cell type. RANK ligand is a cytokine in the TNF family that binds to RANK
on myeloid lineage cells and is central to osteoclast differentiation and activation. Other
osteoclast cytokine signaling pathways also fine-tune bone homeostasis in homeostasis
and disease.67,68 The manner in which cytokines, such as TNF-a, affect overall osteolysis
via macrophage and osteoclast activation versus that of osteoclast activation alone is not
well understood.69 In vitro osteoclasts can phagocytose a wide range of sizes of ceramic,
polymeric, and metallic implant debris particles and remain hormone-responsive and
functional bone-resorbing cells;70,71 however, because of their bone-resorbing
specialization, once fully differentiated, osteoclasts lose their ability to release
inflammatory cytokines.66 This indicates a diminished role for osteoclasts in
perpetuating implant debris–induced inflammation and resultant osteolysis.

temporary changes in the cytokine environment (eg, infection, bone fracture, bone

Chemokines are a subset of cytokines released by phagocytes and dendritic cells in the earliest
phases in response to activating stimuli.
Chemokines are known as chemoattractant cytokines designed to attract and recruit immune
cells to the site of tissue damage, inflammation, or infection.
Chemokines are classified into four main families: C-X-C (α-chemokines), C-C (ß-chemokines),
CX3C (γ-chemokines), and C chemokines (d-chemokines), all of which act via specific G protein-
linked transmembrane chemokine receptors.

fractalkine, and CCL22/MDC.16,81-84

(polymorphonuclear leukocytes).

area; macrophages, natural killer cells, and T cells also are attracted via the CCR2 or CCR4
receptors.79,85
MIP-1α is an adaptive immune response cytokine (T cells and B cells).
CCL17 and CCL22 are important chemokines for adaptive immune responses.86

Therapeutic Regulation of Innate Immune Cytokines
Cytokine or anti-cytokine biologic treatment options in orthopaedics that address the
pathology of aseptic implant loosening largely remain in clinical trials or are under
development specifically for the indication of aseptic osteolysis. Candidate treatment options
include the following:
Inhibition of inflammatory cytokines
AM630 is a selective inhibitor of cannabinoid receptor 2 that inhibits IL-1ß and TNF-a.102
TNF antagonists (eg, etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab) and IL-1 antagonists (eg,
anakinra)103
LY294002 is a specific inhibitor of phosphoinositide 3-kinase that suppresses the
expression of TNF-α.104
Simvastatin decreases extracellular signal-regulated protein kinase 1/2, a phosphorylated
protein that is stimulated by wear particles and involved in cell signaling activation of
macrophages.105
Inhibition of degradative enzymes
Tetracycline inhibits matrix metalloproteinase-9.106
Anti-inflammatory cytokine management
Local delivery of IL-4 to mitigate inflammation-associated bone loss and enhance bone
regeneration.107-109
IL-13 to reduce particle-induced bone and collagen loss and the area of bone surface
covered by tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase–positive osteoclasts.109
Anti-cytokine transduction treatment

Concerns exist regarding long-term off-target immunosuppressive effects of proposed
and current anti-inflammatory therapies.103 Recently developed cytokine-modulating
drugs have shown promise in mouse models, in which local delivery of lentivirus-
mediated TNF-a small interfering RNA molecules resulted in less implant debris–induced
TNF-α, IL-1, and IL-6 and less associated inflammation overall;110 however, most
candidate treatment options are designed to more directly interfere with the production
or action of the more potent proinflammatory cytokines IL-1ß and TNF-α.
Anti-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-4, also are under intense investigation for clinical
use and show promise in modulating M0 and M1 macrophage phenotypes into a
phenotype more similar to M2. Management via IL-4 has shown promise, with M2-like
conversion as evidenced by several M2 markers, including CD206, arginase 1,
downregulation of TNF-α, and increase in IL-1 receptor activator, all of which contribute
to a more anti-inflammatory environment.107,108 IL-13 is another anti-inflammatory
cytokine investigated as a potential treatment option for particle-induced osteolysis. IL-
13 has also shown promise in vivo in reducing particle-induced bone and collagen loss
and in decreasing the area of examined/managed bone surface covered by active
osteoclasts.104
This is no surprise given the potent local actions of cytokines, which are tightly regulated
and generally not available for monitoring in peripheral blood for subtle local events.
Therefore, potent cytokines are not viable systemic biomarkers of early slow or subtle
progressive osteolysis. These same cytokines that may be useful as orthopaedic
biomarkers, at least if conditions are advanced or extreme, also are associated with
numerous other health conditions, including inflammation of most organ systems (eg,
heart, liver, kidney). Local aspiration of joint fluid for biomarker monitoring generally is
not practical because of patient comfort and the risk of infection. Without clinically
